label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Peter, your nine years in payroll are worth listening to, especially on recovery when people leave and the time spent administering an informal scheme. Those are real problems. I also agree that someone taking an advance every month needs more than another advance.

Where I disagree quite strongly is with “it’s painful for one or two pay cycles and then people adjust. They always do.” We tried almost exactly what you’re recommending in 2025, and we ended up reversing it. People did adjust, but some of those adjustments created problems for them and for the business.

Brenda, I’m sharing the figures because this is the evidence I wish I’d had before we closed ours.

We have about 340 staff in logistics, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. Our old arrangement sounds much like yours: informal requests, HR in the middle, and not enough written rules. Finance pushed back on cash flow, repeat borrowing and whether we should be doing this at all. All reasonable questions.

We stopped advances in February 2025. We gave two months’ notice, rather than the three Peter suggests, and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO. So we did not simply shut the door without warning or offer no alternative.

**In the six months after closure, reception logged 61 debt-collector or loan-app calls to the office, up from a handful previously.** Some apps were also calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”.

That is where I struggle with the argument that the loan is the employee’s own contract and therefore outside the company’s business. Legally, it is their contract. Operationally, reception was answering the calls, supervisors were being contacted, and HR was still dealing with the consequences. Stopping advances did not remove that work. Some of it just moved out of payroll and into other people’s working day.

We also saw unplanned absence rise on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers “sorting out” loans.

I’m not claiming that every absence was caused by closing the scheme, or that our experience proves what will happen in every workplace. But these were enough warning signs that we could not honestly say people had adjusted after a couple of pay cycles and the problem had gone away.

One loader at Changamwe was borrowing from six apps by the time he came to me, using one to pay another. It took us four months working with payroll to unwind it. That is one person’s experience, not a statistic for the whole workforce, but it shows what “going elsewhere” can look like. We had stopped providing advances and still ended up spending months dealing with debt.

On SACCOs, I’m not against them. We brought ours in for the financial literacy session because we thought they could help. But their loans take two to three weeks to process and require guarantors. That may work for a planned expense. It does not answer the immediate problem of a child being sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

Financial literacy is useful too. But at KES 28,000 a month, knowing how to budget and having enough money to absorb an emergency are not the same thing. We should offer the education without assuming it makes emergency borrowing unnecessary.

**We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did not reopen the old informal arrangement.** We put a policy in writing:

- Maximum advance of **40% of net pay**.
- Once per pay cycle.
- Repaid in full at the next payroll.
- No fee.
- Requests submitted through the payroll portal, not by coming to my office to plead a case.
- Existing deductions checked before approval, including compliance with the Employment Act’s limit on total deductions of two-thirds of wages.

The 40% net-pay cap is our internal ceiling, not a substitute for the statutory deductions check. An employee does not automatically qualify for the full 40% if their other deductions would make repayment impermissible. Nobody should receive an advance only to be left with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we have been handling about 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. Recovery has been 100% apart from two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year.

So Peter is right that leavers can leave a balance behind. We have had that happen. I would not sell a scheme to Finance as risk-free. But I would put the actual loss on the table alongside the administration involved, then compare it with the absence, missed runs and staff time we were seeing after closure.

The difficulty is that the advance costs are easy to see in one place. The other costs are spread around: reception takes a call, a supervisor gets interrupted, HR handles a debt problem, and operations deals with a missed run. If we only count what sits in payroll, closure can look like a saving without anyone checking the whole picture.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. Not because he has stopped caring about cash flow, but because there is a fixed ceiling and the forecast impact is known in advance. That was a much better answer to his concern than asking him to tolerate an open-ended arrangement.

Brenda, I would therefore separate two questions at your meeting on the 18th: “Should we keep the current informal system?” and “Should we stop salary advances completely?” You can agree with Finance that the first needs to end without agreeing that the second is the only alternative.

I’d take a short written proposal with the cap, frequency, repayment terms and approval route clearly stated. Our 40% may or may not be the right ceiling for your business, but it gives you a concrete starting point. Make payroll responsible for checking eligibility and deductions through a defined process, rather than leaving you to negotiate each request in your office.

Alongside it, take whatever numbers you can pull together before the meeting: how many people currently request advances, how often, the amounts, outstanding balances, losses on exit and the time spent administering them. Ask Finance to cost a capped scheme, not just the existing unlimited one. You could propose a time-limited trial with an agreed review of uptake, recovery, administration and cash flow.

Repeat requests should be part of that review. I agree with Peter that monthly reliance deserves attention. An advance does not increase anyone’s income, and a policy should not pretend otherwise. But frequent use is a reason to understand what is happening, not proof that withdrawing it will improve the employee’s position.

My disagreement, Peter, is not with your concerns about the informal scheme. We had those concerns too. It is with the confidence that closing it means the problem ends after a few uncomfortable months. In our case, it became less visible to Finance and more visible to reception, supervisors and operations.

Brenda’s numbers may lead her to a different decision from ours. But she should go into the 18th with a costed alternative to the current arrangement, not be forced to choose between an open-ended favour system and no help at all.
